column3: Arrogant leaders explicitly reject what the others believed, closely paralleling the social hierarchy behind the focus dialogue.
Disbelief in the Hereafter and adorned deeds produce wandering, providing a related account of misdirected culpability.
It identifies a discernible way of the criminals, supporting the focus's attribution of acquired criminal responsibility.
Arrogant chiefs address the weakened believers, directly staging the same hierarchy, speech, and contested faith.
The immediately preceding ayah has the weakened say that the arrogant prevented their belief, setting up the focus's reply.
Calling a people criminals supports the focus's culpability language but adds no account of leadership or guidance.
The weak confront the arrogant rulers about having followed them and seek relief, a close judgment-scene parallel.
It joins criminality with being lost, reinforcing the focus's connection between culpability and failed guidance.
Guidance has arrived, yet people reject belief because they object to a human messenger.
The weak followers address the arrogant in the Fire and ask whether they can bear any punishment for them.
The next ayah answers the leaders' denial by naming their continual command to disbelief and shared regret.
Criminals acknowledge what they saw and heard too late, giving consequence to the focus's culpability claim.
Recited signs, arrogance, and becoming a criminal people are explicitly joined.
The audience calls Shuayb weak and dismisses his speech, a limited social-power counterpart.
Following those who are guided offers a general positive counterpart to being diverted from guidance.
It treats criminality as a consequence of disbelief after faith, supporting responsibility rather than excuse.
Praise belonging to God indirectly counters the human self-exaltation present in the focus.
Clear proof and guidance have come, and turning away from them incurs punishment, closely framing responsibility after guidance.
God's intention to raise the oppressed contrasts broadly with the focus's weakened followers under arrogant leaders.
True greatness belongs to God, providing a direct corrective to the arrogant status asserted in the focus.
Those who disbelieve and obstruct God's way receive added punishment for spreading corruption.
The alleged leaders deny coercive authority and assign the followers' deviation to their own transgression, almost exactly the focus's defense.
It distinguishes genuinely weakened people who lack means and a route, qualifying the focus's use of weakness.
Protective oaths become a means of obstructing God's way, supplying a concrete form of the blockage disputed in the focus.
Its designation of a criminal people adds only the focus's general culpability vocabulary.
Satan adorns their deeds, blocks them from the path, and leaves them unguided, a clear account of obstructed guidance.
Their ultimate loss offers a broad consequence for criminal wrongdoing without the focus's social dialogue.
The criminal people designation has only a general relation to the focus's charge of criminality.
Those claiming weakness are questioned about failing to leave despite an available land, sharply connecting weakness with responsibility.
The punishment image does not clarify obstruction, guidance, or the allocation of responsibility.
Pharaoh and his elite are arrogant and criminal despite receiving signs, joining elite pride with culpable rejection.
Knowledge of what is hidden and manifest gives only an indirect counterpoint to concealed misguidance.
God knows what the arrogant conceal and reveal, while rejecting their pride as accountable conduct.
It contrasts satanic bewilderment with companions calling a person back to guidance, directly treating social influence and direction.
Migration finds room and alternatives in God's way, complementing the question whether weakness leaves a route of escape.
The arrival of a promised consequence does not illuminate the focus's guidance or blame exchange.
A clear book and light have come to disclose what was concealed, giving an evidentiary counterpart to guidance's arrival.
A clear messenger has come, making later failure to remember a response to received evidence.
A human messenger brings warning, but the ayah does not develop obstruction or the blame between leaders and followers.
Selling God's signs cheaply becomes an act of blocking others from His way.
A demand for a special sign is exposed because earlier messengers brought clear proofs, highlighting culpable refusal after evidence.
Refusal to believe in God's signs is paired with not being guided and with punishment.
After guidance becomes clear, people turn back while Satan makes the retreat attractive.
Those who disbelieve call truth magic when it comes, a limited counterpart to rejecting received guidance.
Guidance to faith is God's gift rather than a status claim, challenging self-credit in religious response.
Criminals confront the Hell they denied, adding a direct consequence for the focus's criminal designation.
Disbelievers obstruct God's way and oppose the messenger after guidance has become clear.
The reference to criminals is too brief to specify how responsibility or obstruction operates.
Truth is labeled sorcery when it arrives, broadly echoing resistance to received guidance.
The vindication of truth against falsehood supplies only a general opposition to criminal resistance.
It explicitly warns against being prevented from God's signs after they have been revealed.
Previous peoples denied despite messengers bringing clear proofs and illuminating scripture.
Being upon guidance is stated without the focus's contested social influence or responsibility.
Following ancestral traces is asserted to be guidance, showing a socially inherited but untested orientation.
Prior obstruction must not produce further transgression, preserving personal responsibility amid a wrong done by others.
Feigning belief serves as a shield while its users obstruct others from God's way.
Disbelief together with blocking God's way is described as far-reaching error.
God's recurring treatment of criminals reinforces that criminality carries a consequential judgment.
Rejecters of received truth expel the messenger and believers because of their faith, illustrating social pressure against belief.
Criminals are separated out for judgment, a consequence of the culpability named in the focus.
Companions block people from the path while persuading them that they are guided.
Inventing lies about God and denying truth once it arrives combines false direction with culpable rejection.
Repeating the speech of earlier deniers offers only a general pattern of inherited refusal.
A person comes striving, giving only a distant positive counterpart to receiving guidance.
The challenge to idolaters does not clarify the focus's hierarchy, guidance, or blame.
The sudden arrival of punishment is not a focused parallel to the disputed obstruction of guidance.
Arrogant chiefs threaten to expel the messenger and believers or force their return to the old religion.
The brothers' denial of theft does not clarify the focus relation.
The arrogant answer their followers in Hell that all are in it and that God has judged between servants.
The gathering of criminals at resurrection gives only a general judgment consequence.
Those who reject meeting God demand extraordinary access and are explicitly charged with arrogance.
Criminal hearts receive the message without accepting it, connecting exposure to revelation with culpable response.
Followers accuse their leaders of having approached them from a position of influence, leading into the same denial of responsibility.
God's guidance cannot be overturned, but this does not address the focus's social causation dispute.
The leaders reply that the followers were not believers, directly matching the focus's shift of blame to them.
Belief in the messenger and following him are presented as the path to guidance.
A close companion leads someone away from the Reminder after it has already come.
Criminals appear chained on the judgment day, a concrete consequence for acquired wrongdoing.
Responding to God and the messenger after hardship is a limited positive counterpart to faithful response.
Faith unmingled with wrongdoing brings security and guidance, contrasting with criminal deviation.
People are threatened and prevented from God's way at every path, while believers are targeted directly.
A group cannot avail against God's judgment, only broadly paralleling the failure of leaders to bear followers' punishment.
In the same surah, clear verses are recast as an attempt to turn people from ancestral worship.
People knowingly block believers from God's way and seek to make that way crooked.
Following luxury rather than restraining corruption ends in becoming criminal, a broad social-responsibility parallel.
The enduring punishment of criminals adds only the focus's general consequence.
Social approval pressures the messenger to follow others' way despite divine guidance already received.
The account groups Pharaoh and earlier peoples under wrongdoing without the focus's guidance or blame dynamics.
Messengers bring clear signs, yet people arrogantly deny some and kill others when the message opposes their desires.
Loss in the Hereafter is a general consequence that does not develop the focal dialogue.
An unsupported exclusivist claim does not clarify obstruction, guidance, or delegated blame.
Human beings are shown the two evident paths, preserving the possibility of responsible choice.
The bare accusation of being bewitched has no focused relation to the dialogue in 34:32.
Guided messengers trust God and endure harm, supplying a positive counterpart to pressure against guidance.
The division into three groups is too general to clarify the focus relation.
Clear proofs precede punishment of criminals, grounding responsibility in a message that has arrived.
The resurrection analogy does not clarify the focus's social or moral causation.
The book is made guidance and prohibits taking another protector, but the link to the blame dialogue is indirect.
Concealing divine testimony is a limited counterpart to refusing truth after knowledge.
The way is shown, while gratitude or disbelief remains the recipient's response, directly supporting responsibility after guidance.
Whenever a warner comes to a town, its affluent elite reject the message, directly extending the surah's portrayal of socially powerful rejecters.
The wealthy rejecters treat wealth and children as proof against punishment, clarifying the social confidence behind elite denial.
Later communities accuse earlier ones of having led them astray and ask for their punishment to be doubled, directly paralleling delegated blame.
Satan denies coercive authority, admits only that he called and they responded, and tells followers not to blame him, closely matching the focus's dispute over causation.
Those who lead others astray without knowledge bear their own burdens together with burdens from those they mislead.
Disbelievers urge believers to follow their way and promise to carry their sins, making deceptive social influence explicit.
Those who mislead others bear their own burdens and additional burdens from those they have led astray.
Followers confess obeying their leaders and great ones, then say those authorities led them from the way.
The followers ask that their leaders receive a double punishment and curse for having led them astray.
The condemned turn to one another in questioning, framing the same mutual recrimination developed in the following verses.
The leaders and followers are jointly subject to the word of punishment, qualifying the unilateral blame defense in 34:32.
Leaders concede that they led their followers astray because they themselves were astray, a direct contrast to the denial in 34:32.
Leaders and followers share the punishment, preserving both influence and individual culpability.
Those who were followed disown their followers when punishment appears, severing the very relation on which followers relied.
A people who went astray and led many others astray are explicitly named as a warning against following their desires.
Devils among humans and jinn adorn deceptive speech for one another, supplying a broader model of socially mediated misdirection.
Pharaoh leads his people on the Day of Resurrection into the Fire, directly depicting a leader's destructive guidance.
Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them, an explicit political-leadership counterpart.
The speaker regrets taking a particular person as an intimate companion, supplying the relational premise for being diverted from the Reminder.
Satan has led a great multitude astray, directly linking large-scale influence to failed judgment.
Those who disbelieve ask to be shown the humans and jinn who led them astray, extending the judgment-scene assignment of blame.
Elites defend their orientation by claiming to follow their ancestors' way, showing inherited authority presented as guidance.
Turning away from the Reminder results in a satanic companion, providing a clear mechanism of accompanying misdirection.
Pharaoh misleads his people and they obey him, directly joining ruler influence with follower compliance.
Opponents attempt to turn the messenger away from what was revealed to him, an explicit effort to obstruct revealed guidance.
Elites press for believers to be excluded, illustrating status-based pressure against a community organized around remembrance.
Satan declares that he will sit on God's straight path to obstruct those traveling it.
Satan approaches people from every direction to divert their response from gratitude, expanding the focus's question of harmful influence.
Moses identifies Pharaoh and his chiefs' wealth and splendor as a means by which people are led astray from God's way.
Associates are set up to lead people astray from God's way, explicitly joining false authority with misdirection.
Satan gains mastery, makes people forget God's remembrance, and organizes them as his party.
Satan tells a person to disbelieve and then disowns him once he does, a close pattern of incitement followed by denial of responsibility.
